question: Tell me about a challenging project you worked on and your role in it.
assesses: Problem-solving under difficulty and personal ownership. The question asks for two things -- the challenge and the candidate's role in it -- so an answer that describes the project without establishing what the candidate personally did has only half-answered it.
good_answer: Set out the project and the specific difficulty briefly, then spend most of the answer on the candidate's own decisions and actions in response to that difficulty, and close with the outcome and what it produced. The interviewer should be able to state afterwards what the candidate was responsible for and what they did about the problem.
common_pitfalls: Never states the candidate's role, even though the question explicitly asks for it
Describes the work in the first-person plural throughout, so the individual contribution stays invisible
Narrates the project chronologically without ever identifying what made it difficult
Presents an ordinary constraint such as a busy period as the challenge, which shows little
Ends with a self-assessment such as everything went well instead of a stated outcome
feedback_hints: If the role is never stated, say so first -- this is the part of the question that was missed
If the answer is dominated by 'we', ask for the specific decisions the candidate made themselves
If the difficulty amounted to working longer hours, suggest identifying the real obstacle, such as a technical problem or a conflicting requirement
If the outcome is only a general claim of success, suggest stating what concretely changed as a result
source: Prospects.ac.uk (competency-based interviews); STAR guidance, UK National Careers Service

question: Describe a time you had a conflict with a teammate and how you handled it.
assesses: Handling interpersonal disagreement at work. The competency being scored is the handling -- what the candidate did to address the disagreement with the other person -- not whether the conflict was resolved in their favour.
good_answer: State the disagreement and what was actually at stake, then describe the steps taken to address it directly with the other person, and finish with how it was resolved and what the candidate took from it. Keeping the description of the colleague fair and factual matters: the interviewer is assessing the candidate's conduct, not judging the absent party.
common_pitfalls: Working around the problem, for example taking on the work alone, which avoids the conflict rather than handling it
Blaming the colleague throughout, which tells the interviewer about the candidate's attitude rather than their skill
Describing only how frustrating the situation felt, with no account of what was done
Choosing an example so minor that no real disagreement had to be handled
feedback_hints: If the candidate solved it by absorbing the work themselves, point out that this bypasses the conflict and ask what conversation they had with the colleague
If the answer is largely criticism of the other person, suggest refocusing on the candidate's own actions and the steps they initiated
If feelings dominate the answer, ask for the specific steps taken and the outcome they led to
source: Prospects.ac.uk (competency-based interviews, conflict at work); Levashina et al. (2014)

question: Why are you interested in this position?
assesses: Motivation and how well the candidate has researched the role. The interviewer wants evidence that this application is specific to this role and organisation, and that the candidate has something to offer it.
good_answer: Connect something concrete about the role or organisation to the candidate's own experience and goals, showing evidence of research, and make clear what the candidate would bring as well as what they hope to gain.
common_pitfalls: Praise that would apply to any large employer, with nothing specific to this one
Framing the role purely as a personal learning opportunity, with nothing offered in return
Reciting facts about the organisation without connecting them to the candidate's own experience
Focusing on conditions such as pay or location rather than the work itself
Answering about the field in general rather than this particular position
feedback_hints: If the reasons would fit any employer, suggest naming something specific about this role or organisation
If the answer is entirely about what the candidate would gain, suggest adding what they would contribute
If facts about the organisation are listed without a link, suggest tying each one to the candidate's own experience
If the answer describes the industry rather than the role, point out that the question asked about this position
source: Prospects.ac.uk (interview questions); UK National Careers Service (interview advice)

question: Tell me about a skill you recently learned, and how you learned it.
assesses: Capacity and motivation to learn, and how deliberately the candidate goes about it. The question asks both what was learned and the process, so the method matters as much as the skill.
good_answer: Name the skill and why it was worth learning, describe how it was learned including what was difficult and how that was worked through, and show that it has actually been applied to something.
common_pitfalls: Names the skill but says nothing about how it was learned, which is half the question
Claims a broad skill on the basis of a short course, with no evidence of use
Describes the learning as effortless, so the interviewer learns nothing about how obstacles are handled
Never applies the skill to anything, leaving it as a claim rather than a demonstrated capability
feedback_hints: If the method is missing, point out that the question asked how it was learned
If nothing was difficult, ask what was hardest and how it was worked through
If the skill has not been applied, suggest describing where it was used and what it produced
If the claim is broad but the evidence is a single course, suggest scoping the claim to what was actually done
source: Prospects.ac.uk (competency-based interviews); UK National Careers Service (interview advice)

question: Give an example of a time you led a team.
assesses: Leadership in practice: how the candidate set direction, organised other people and handled the problems that arose. Formal authority is not required -- what is scored is the leading behaviour.
good_answer: Set out the goal and the team briefly, then concentrate on what the candidate did as the leader -- how work was allocated, how people were kept aligned, how a difficulty or disagreement was handled -- and close with the result and what was learned about leading.
common_pitfalls: Reports the team's achievement without describing any leading behaviour
States the job title rather than showing what leading actually involved
Skips the hard part, so the interviewer never sees how the candidate handles people problems
Claims credit for the whole team's work rather than describing how others were enabled
feedback_hints: If the answer describes the outcome but not the leading, ask how work was allocated and how the team was kept on track
If a title is offered as evidence, suggest replacing it with a specific thing the candidate did as leader
If nothing went wrong in the story, ask what the hardest moment was and how it was handled
If the candidate claims the team's output as their own, suggest showing how they enabled others to deliver it

question: Tell me about a time you failed or made a mistake, and what you did next.
assesses: Accountability and learning from experience. The question has two halves -- the failure and the response -- and the response is what is really being scored.
good_answer: Choose a real failure with genuine consequences, state plainly what went wrong and the candidate's part in it, then focus on what was done to address it and what changed in their practice afterwards. An outcome that stayed negative is acceptable provided the response and the learning are clear.
common_pitfalls: Chooses something that is not really a failure, such as working too hard, which avoids the question
Attributes the failure to other people or circumstances, so no accountability is shown
Describes the failure at length but says little about what was done afterwards
States a general lesson such as learning to communicate better without any change in behaviour to show for it
feedback_hints: If the example is not a genuine failure, point out that the question asks for a real one and that a candid answer scores better
If responsibility is placed elsewhere, ask what the candidate's own part in it was
If the answer stops at the failure, point out that the second half of the question -- what was done next -- is the part being assessed
If the lesson is abstract, ask what the candidate does differently now as a result
source: Prospects.ac.uk (interview questions, failure and achievement); Levashina et al. (2014)

question: Tell me about a time you had to meet a tight deadline or manage competing priorities.
assesses: Planning, prioritisation and judgement under pressure. What is scored is the basis on which the candidate decided what came first, and what they did about the rest.
good_answer: Describe the competing demands and the constraint, explain how the candidate decided what to prioritise and on what basis, mention what was renegotiated, delegated or dropped, and give the outcome.
common_pitfalls: Resolves everything by working longer hours, which shows effort rather than prioritisation
Says the work was prioritised without explaining the basis for the decisions
Ignores the trade-off -- nothing was ever renegotiated, delegated or dropped
Leaves out whether the deadline was actually met and at what cost
feedback_hints: If the solution was extra hours, ask how the candidate decided what mattered most
If prioritisation is asserted, ask what criteria were used to rank the work
If no trade-off appears, ask what was renegotiated, delegated or set aside
If the outcome is missing, point out that the interviewer needs to know whether the deadline was met
